nameStory: The bog bilberry gets its name from its preferred wetland home and its close kinship to European bilberries. 'Bilberry' comes from the Danish 'bøllebar' meaning 'dark berry,' referring to the deep blue-purple fruits that were prized by Northern European cultures for centuries.
description: Bog bilberry is a low-growing shrub that hugs the ground in acidic wetlands, rarely reaching more than 2 feet tall. This hardy member of the blueberry family produces small, pale pink bell-shaped flowers in spring, followed by dark blue berries with a whitish bloom. Its oval leaves are blue-green with a distinctive pale underside, and the whole plant has a compact, spreading growth habit perfect for surviving in harsh bog conditions.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are distinctly blue-green on top with conspicuously pale, almost whitish undersides - flip a leaf over and the contrast is striking. The leaves feel smooth and somewhat thick, lacking the tiny teeth that edge most blueberry leaves.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue berries are covered with a whitish, waxy bloom that rubs off easily when touched. The berries taste sweet but somewhat bland compared to cultivated blueberries, with a slightly mealy texture.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, pale pink to white bell-shaped flowers dangle singly or in small clusters. Each flower has four petals (unlike the five-petaled flowers of most blueberries) and feels waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats rarely over 2 feet tall, with multiple woody stems branching close to the ground. The plant has a distinctly horizontal growth pattern, spreading outward rather than growing upright.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems have smooth, reddish-brown bark that feels firm but not rough. Young twigs are often reddish and smooth to the touch, lacking the fuzzy texture found on some blueberry species.

habitat: Look for bog bilberry in acidic wetlands like sphagnum bogs, wet meadows, and the edges of mountain ponds, especially at higher elevations. It thrives in constantly moist, nutrient-poor soils alongside sphagnum moss, Labrador tea, and other bog specialists. In New England, it's most common in the northern regions and higher elevations where cool, wet conditions persist.

seasonality.spring: Pale pink bell-shaped flowers appear in late spring, usually May to early June. Look for the distinctive four-petaled flowers hanging beneath the blue-green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Dark blue berries ripen from July through August, covered in their characteristic whitish bloom. The blue-green leaves with pale undersides are most easily observed during the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of red, orange, and purple, creating stunning displays in bog landscapes. Some berries may persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Deciduous plant loses its leaves, leaving bare reddish-brown twigs in spreading, horizontal patterns across the bog surface.

funFact: Bog bilberry flowers typically have only four petals instead of the five found in most of its blueberry relatives - this unusual trait makes it one of the few four-petaled members of a predominantly five-petaled plant family!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with lowbush blueberry, but bog bilberry's pale leaf undersides are the dead giveaway - lowbush blueberry leaves are green on both sides. Remember: 'bog bilberry shows its pale belly' when you flip the leaves over.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bilberry,' this North American species is distinct from the true European bilberry, though they're closely related. The name can cause confusion for foragers familiar with European bilberries, as the flavors and growing habits differ significantly.
compareHints: Unlike lowbush blueberry which has green leaf undersides and toothed leaf edges, bog bilberry has distinctly pale leaf undersides and smooth-edged leaves. It also grows in much wetter conditions than most of its Vaccinium relatives and has the unusual four-petaled flowers rather than the typical five petals of other blueberries and cranberries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Vaccinium cousins, lingonberry is evergreen while blueberries lose their leaves in winter.
Differs from highbush blueberry mainly by size - lowbush stays under 2 feet while highbush can reach 6-12 feet tall.
American cranberry is much more robust than its cousin bog cranberry, with leaves twice the size and significantly larger berries.
Among its Vaccinium relatives, northern highbush blueberry is easily the tallest – lowbush blueberry stays under 2 feet, while lingonberry and the various cranberries are ground-hugging plants.
Among New England blueberries, velvetleaf blueberry is the only one with distinctly fuzzy leaves - lowbush and highbush blueberries have smooth, hairless leaves.

Among its Vaccinium relatives, bog cranberry is distinguished by its extremely small size and creeping habit - while lowbush blueberries also stay low, they form upright clumps rather than trailing mats.
Unlike highbush blueberries that grow tall and upright, early lowbush stays under 3 feet and spreads horizontally.
Among New England's blueberries, black highbush stands out for its distinctively dark berries and fuzzy stems and leaves.
Unlike lowbush and highbush blueberries which have stamens that stay tucked inside their flowers, deerberry's stamens prominently stick out like tiny antennae.
Unlike its lowland cousins like lowbush blueberry and highbush blueberry, dwarf bilberry stays extremely small and produces single berries instead of clusters.
Compared to lowbush blueberry, northern blueberry prefers cooler climates and higher elevations, with slightly rounder leaves and often more intense berry flavor.
